column3: Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses singular collective “the Amorite”; BSB uses plural “the Amorites.”
The Hebrew describes the people with a singular collective pronoun; BSB uses plural “they.”
The Hebrew makes singular Moab the speaker and repeats the licking verb for the assembly and the ox; BSB uses “the Moabites” and varies “devour” with “licks up.”

The Hebrew names “the river” and “the eye of the land,” repeats “Behold,” and leaves the sender unnamed in the narrative clause. BSB identifies the river as the Euphrates, uses “the face of the land,” and explicitly names Balak as the speaker.
The Hebrew compares the people as “mightier than I” and changes from “I may be able” to plural “we shall strike”; BSB uses “too mighty for me” and keeps the defeat action singular.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed; BSB supplies “Balaam.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says Balak “sent to me,” without an explicit “this message”; BSB supplies that object.
The Hebrew calls the land’s surface its “eye”; BSB says “the face of the land.”
The Hebrew uses singular collective “it is blessed” for the people; BSB uses plural “they are blessed.”
The Hebrew says “in the morning” and “Go to your land”; BSB adds “next” and “back.”
The Hebrew says the princes “came to Balak”; BSB says they “returned.”
The Hebrew compares the later princes with “these”; BSB explicitly supplies “the first messengers.”
The Hebrew asks Balaam not to withhold himself from going; BSB asks that nothing hinder him.
The Hebrew emphasizes honoring with a repeated verb and says “very much”; BSB says “honor you richly.”
The Hebrew says not to pass beyond “the mouth of the LORD”; BSB says “the command of the LORD.”
The Hebrew says “you also” should stay the night; BSB explains this as “as the others did.”
The Hebrew introduces the men’s arrival with “if”; BSB uses “Since.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew refers to Balaam with pronouns in both the going and riding clauses; BSB supplies his name in both places.
The Hebrew names “the donkey” three times; BSB names her once and then uses pronouns.
The Hebrew describes a vineyard path with “a wall on this side and a wall on that side”; BSB specifies “between two vineyards” and combines the walls as “on either side.”
The Hebrew repeats “the wall”; BSB replaces the second occurrence with “it.”
The Hebrew joins right and left with “and”; BSB uses “or.”
The Hebrew repeats Balaam’s name as the one becoming angry; BSB uses “he.”
